summary:
ARES is a full-stack, interactive 2D/3D planetary GIS and autonomous navigation web application designed for Mars exploration. Built with Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, Leaflet, and Globe.gl, it features bilingual (Ukrainian/English) support and cloud route synchronization.
To solve complex off-world traversal challenges, the platform integrates NASA Mars Trek imagery and MOLA elevation models with an any-angle A* pathfinding engine smoothed via Elastic Band and Catmull-Rom algorithms. Users can compare "Safe" and "Fast" routes that dynamically avoid steep slopes, craters, hazardous zones, and moving dust storms modeled on MRO/MARCI climatology. Additionally, it provides real-time crew supply calculations (oxygen, fuel, food, and water), an emergency SOS evacuation router, Waze-style crowdsourced hazard alerts, and a live astronaut radio chat.
Because Earth–Mars communication delays prevent real-time teleoperation, autonomous pathfinding and hazard forecasting are vital for planetary missions. This tool minimizes mission-ending terrain and weather risks while optimizing life-support logistics to keep future robotic and crewed expeditions safe.
details:
ARES is a full-stack, interactive 2D/3D planetary Geographic Information System (GIS) and autonomous navigation web application built for Martian surface exploration.
Users can switch seamlessly between a tactical 2D topographical map and an interactive 3D Martian globe layered with real NASA Mars Trek imagery and Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) elevation models. When a user sets a start point and destination, the routing engine runs an any-angle A* pathfinding algorithm refined with Elastic Band and Catmull-Rom spline smoothing to generate natural, continuous driving trajectories rather than jagged grid paths.
Key operational features include:
Dual Routing Profiles ("Safe" vs. "Fast"): Evaluates terrain slope gradients, crater rims, hazardous zones, and dynamic, moving dust storms modeled on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) and Mars Color Imager (MARCI) climatology.
Real-Time Crew Supply Telemetry: Calculates oxygen, fuel, food, and water consumption dynamically based on route distance, elevation gain, and estimated travel time.
Emergency SOS Evacuation Router: Instantly recalculates the safest, fastest escape path to the nearest safe zone or base camp during critical failures or approaching storms.
Crowdsourced Hazard Alerts & Radio Chat: Lets expedition members drop Waze-style hazard pins on newly discovered obstacles, synchronize routes via the cloud, and coordinate through a built-in live astronaut radio chat.
Bilingual Interface: Full localization in both English and Ukrainian.
Benefits
Overcomes Communication Latency: Because one-way signal delays between Earth and Mars range from 4 to 24 minutes, real-time teleoperation is impossible. On-site autonomous pathfinding allows crews and rovers to make immediate navigation decisions without waiting for Earth-based mission control.
Reduces Mechanical and Environmental Risk: Automated slope analysis and dust storm forecasting prevent vehicles from tipping on steep inclines, getting trapped in craters, or losing power and visibility inside severe weather systems.
Prevents Resource Depletion: Coupling terrain routing directly with life-support math ensures expeditions never embark on a traverse that exceeds their oxygen, water, food, or fuel reserves.
Streamlines Multi-Crew Coordination: Cloud-synced routes, shared hazard markers, and live radio communication keep multiple rovers or field teams aligned on changing surface conditions.
Intended Impact
Mars Rover Pathfinder is designed to bridge the gap between raw planetary datasets and practical mission operations. For future robotic scouts and crewed expeditions—such as those envisioned under NASA's Moon to Mars architecture—the platform demonstrates how autonomous terrain-aware routing and integrated life-support tracking can dramatically improve surface survivability and mission efficiency. Beyond mission simulation, it serves as an accessible educational tool that lets students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore real Martian topography and experience the real engineering constraints of off-world navigation.
Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used
Programming Languages: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3, SQL
Frontend & 2D/3D Visualization:
Leaflet.js for interactive 2D planetary GIS mapping and custom overlays
Globe.gl and Three.js for hardware-accelerated 3D Martian globe rendering
Backend & Cloud Infrastructure:
Node.js and Express.js for RESTful API routing, pathfinding services, and live radio messaging
PostgreSQL for persistent cloud storage of saved routes, telemetry logs, and crowdsourced hazard alerts
Algorithms & Scientific Datasets:
Custom any-angle A* pathfinding, Elastic Band trajectory optimization, and Catmull-Rom spline interpolation
NASA Mars Trek basemap imagery, MOLA digital elevation models, and MRO/MARCI dust storm climatology data
Development Environment & Hardware: Developed on Windows 11 workstations using Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub for version control, and modern browser WebGL debugging tools.
How the Project Is Creative
Rather than presenting Martian elevation data as a static scientific viewer, Mars Rover Pathfinder reimagines planetary exploration through the lens of modern terrestrial navigation apps. It blends rigorous aerospace data—such as MOLA elevation gradients and MARCI seasonal dust storm models—with intuitive, human-centered concepts like "Safe vs. Fast" route comparisons, Waze-style crowdsourced hazard reporting, and a one-tap SOS evacuation mode. Uniting 2D tactical GIS planning, 3D orbital visualization, dynamic weather hazards, and real-time human survival logistics inside a single lightweight web application turns complex planetary data into an interactive mission command center.
Factors Considered
Martian Terrain & Vehicle Limits: Steep crater walls, loose regolith, and extreme elevation changes directly govern rover stability, speed, and energy draw; slope thresholds were weighted heavily in the pathfinding cost function.
Dynamic Weather Hazards: Mars experiences regional and global dust storms that threaten solar power generation, thermal stability, and visibility, requiring time-aware storm movement rather than static obstacle maps.
Crew Survival Margins: For human missions, the shortest distance is not always survivable if steep climbs exhaust fuel and oxygen faster than flat detours; supply consumption was modeled directly alongside distance.
Earth–Mars Delay: Every navigation, rerouting, and emergency evacuation feature was engineered to run independently without requiring real-time input from Earth.
Usability & Accessibility: High-contrast overlays, clear 2D/3D view switching, and native English/Ukrainian support ensure critical telemetry remains readable under high-stress mission scenarios.
